items.title: OpenAI shares ten major advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science achieved by its AI model Astra, including disproving longstanding conjectures and improving bounds in multiple fields [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI announced that its internal AI model Astra has made significant progress on ten longstanding open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, spanning areas such as high-dimensional geometry, coding theory, group theory, quantum complexity, and lattice cryptography. These results include disproving the Erdős unit-distance conjecture and Connes's rigidity conjecture, establishing the existence of non-sofic groups, and providing new bounds on sphere packing and arithmetic circuit complexity. The AI-generated proofs were formalized and verified using the Lean proof assistant, with human researchers preparing the manuscripts. OpenAI emphasizes its commitment to transparency and responsibility, acknowledging the collaborative role of AI and humans in producing these results and encouraging the mathematical community to engage with and build upon these findings. The initiative also includes providing free access to advanced AI tools for academic researchers to accelerate discovery.

items.title: Developer advocates manually retyping LLM-generated code to prevent cognitive debt and maintain understanding in personal projects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer describes a workflow where they manually type out code generated by large language models (LLMs) instead of directly copying it, aiming to maintain a deep understanding of their projects and avoid accumulating cognitive debt. They instruct their coding assistant to show proposed edits and commands in chat rather than automatically applying them, allowing for careful review and comprehension. This approach slows down development compared to fully automated code generation but helps the developer build a mental model of the codebase, detect errors or hallucinations, and adapt the code to their preferences. The developer compares this method to traditional learning advice of typing out code examples to better understand them and plans to continue this practice to balance productivity with comprehension.

items.title: AirLLM enables 70B parameter LLM inference on a single 4GB GPU without quantization or pruning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AirLLM is an open-source project that significantly reduces memory usage during inference, allowing large language models with up to 70 billion parameters to run on a single 4GB GPU. It achieves this without relying on quantization, distillation, or pruning techniques, and supports even larger models like Llama 3.1 405B on 8GB and DeepSeek-V3 671B on about 12GB by streaming sparse MoE model experts one at a time. The project includes features such as model compression for up to 3x inference speed improvements, support for various popular models including Qwen, Llama 3.x/4, and DeepSeek versions, and compatibility with MacOS. AirLLM also offers tools for automatic model detection and loading, and supports CPU inference and non-sharded models, making it accessible for a wide range of hardware configurations.

items.title: Researchers introduce Counterfactual-Faithful Quantization to improve algorithmic recourse stability in quantized models, reducing recourse failures and intervention costs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Model quantization reduces memory and latency but can disrupt algorithmic recourse by invalidating small actionable changes that flip decisions in full-precision models. This study proposes counterfactual sensitivity metrics-Validity Drop and Counterfactual Recourse Gap-to measure how quantization affects recourse behavior and introduces Counterfactual-Faithful Quantization (CFQ), a training method that preserves recourse outcomes while optimizing quantizer parameters and bit allocation. CFQ is compatible with standard quantizers and can be applied as a training-free calibration for post-training quantization. Experiments on datasets including Adult, German Credit, and COMPAS demonstrate that while standard quantization methods maintain accuracy, they degrade recourse stability; CFQ consistently reduces recourse failures and cost increases at matched accuracy and bit budgets, improving recourse reliability in compressed models.

items.title: DRIFT framework improves large language model self-improvement with difficulty routing and rhythm gating, achieving new state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose DRIFT, an online self-evolution policy optimization framework for large language models that dynamically adjusts training signals based on problem difficulty and focuses exploration on critical reasoning tokens. DRIFT incorporates a success buffer and a two-stage curriculum learning strategy to preserve high-quality experience and guide stable policy evolution. Evaluated on five benchmarks and three model scales, DRIFT outperforms previous methods GRPO and SDPO, achieving an average score of 79.5% and setting new state-of-the-art accuracy of 79.2% on the ToolUse benchmark.

items.title: Researchers propose ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework for traceable context reconstruction in agentic reinforcement learning, improving accuracy and efficiency on BrowseComp-Plus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce ECHO, a framework designed to improve long-horizon language agents' decision-making by selectively compressing and reconstructing past interactions with source-indexed memory records. This approach addresses the challenge of assigning credit to relevant evidence in bounded context windows during reinforcement learning. ECHO outperforms previous methods like GRPO and SUPO on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, achieving 43.4% held-out accuracy while using fewer turns and less trajectory data. The trained policy also demonstrates improved zero-shot generalization across various tasks, including multi-objective question answering, code generation, and information-seeking benchmarks on both dense and mixture-of-experts backbones.

items.title: Researchers find cheap open-weight models can reliably judge natural-language mathematical proofs at up to 100 times lower cost than frontier LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated whether inexpensive open-weight models can effectively grade natural-language mathematical proofs compared to expensive large language model (LLM) judges. On a 200-instance validation set from IMO-GradingBench, three low-cost models-GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek-V4 Flash, and Gemma-4 31B-matched human pass/fail decisions at rates statistically indistinguishable from leading models Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, while costing up to 100 times less. Extending the evaluation to the full 1000-instance benchmark, they found that requiring unanimous agreement among the three cheap judges yielded the highest precision and consistency across multiple runs. The study suggests that these affordable models can serve as competitive automated judges for mathematical proofs, significantly reducing evaluation costs. The recommended consensus rule, requiring all three judges to pass a proof, was identified post-hoc and the authors note it requires independent replication before widespread adoption.

items.title: MemoryForge introduces lifelong memory synthesis for LLM agents to enable human-like behaviors in role-play and user simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: MemoryForge is a new framework that equips large language models (LLMs) with human-like personas by synthesizing lifelong autobiographical memory from brief target personas. Unlike traditional methods that use static textual profiles, MemoryForge enables frozen LLMs to dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memories to guide their behavior, improving realism in agentic applications such as role-play and user simulation. The framework includes a context generator for socio-historical grounding, a life organizer for developmental coherence, and a multi-resolution simulator balancing broad summaries with detailed episodic experiences. Experiments on PersonaGym and SimulatorArena demonstrate that MemoryForge's synthesized memory base helps frozen LLMs exhibit more human-like behaviors than strong descriptive conditioning baselines across multiple metrics and model backbones.

items.title: Researchers introduce Obshazard-bench to evaluate multimodal foundation models for real-time disaster intelligence using raw Earth observation data across 8 disaster categories in over 60 countries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed Obshazard-bench, a real-time benchmark designed to assess multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in interpreting raw Earth observation data for disaster emergency response. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on static, expert-processed data, Obshazard-bench integrates high-frequency satellite streams with ground observations, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators to better reflect operational disaster scenarios. The benchmark covers 8 major disaster categories and 28 sub-categories across more than 60 countries, including over 120 documented extreme events and thousands of visual question answering samples. It defines a three-stage evaluation aligned with disaster workflows: Predictive Crisis Anticipation, Active Evolution Reasoning, and Multi-faceted Impact Quantification. Experiments reveal significant challenges for current foundation models in converting raw multi-channel observations into timely and decision-relevant disaster insights.

items.title: Researchers propose LLM-OSDA, a dynamic cost-per-click auction integrating optimal stopping for native ads in multi-turn LLM conversations, improving revenue by 11% over fixed-timing baselines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: LLM-OSDA is a new auction mechanism designed to embed native advertising within multi-turn large language model (LLM) conversations by dynamically determining the optimal timing to insert ads based on bids and contextual click quality. Unlike existing single-response ad auctions, LLM-OSDA couples timing and allocation decisions using Bellman optimal stopping and envelope pricing, ensuring truthful bidding is weakly dominant in expectation under an exact oracle. The system uses a learned StopNet to approximate optimal stopping decisions, with experiments on simulated conversational ad data showing an 11% net revenue increase compared to fixed-timing methods while maintaining similar user retention. This approach shifts the advertising unit from fixed slots to moments within evolving conversations, addressing challenges in timing and allocation coupling for LLM-native ads.

items.title: Researchers introduce OSCD algorithm to improve native multilingual chain-of-thought reasoning in low-resource Southeast Asian languages, achieving up to 3.2 times better mathematical reasoning performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Large Language Models often revert to English during complex reasoning in low-resource native languages, limiting their effectiveness. Researchers propose the Onramp-Sequence Cross-Distillation (OSCD) algorithm, which projects high-resource reasoning paths into low-resource vocabularies and aligns semantic embeddings to bridge cross-lingual gaps. Evaluations on AIME25 and HMMT25 benchmarks show OSCD improves mathematical reasoning in Southeast Asian languages by up to 3.2 times, with semantic alignment contributing up to 6.4% improvement in reducing linguistic bias compared to translation-only methods.

items.title: Researchers propose Test-Time Context Distillation to improve long-context language modeling by guiding models to retain information relevant for future predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Test-Time Context Distillation (TTCD), a framework that uses a long-window teacher to supervise a short-window student model, enabling better allocation of limited memory for future token prediction in long-context language tasks. The in-place variant, IP-TTCD, leverages existing model parameters for fast adaptation and outperforms prior methods like DeltaNet and sliding-window attention when trained from scratch. IP-TTCD also allows pre-trained transformers to adapt during inference with minimal architectural changes, advancing continual learning approaches for long-context capabilities.

items.title: Researchers develop first general-purpose macronizer for Ancient Greek vowel length annotation using recursive modules and transformer training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have created the first general-purpose tool to automatically annotate vowel length in Ancient Greek texts, addressing the lack of large-scale macronized corpora. The system uses lemma, part-of-speech, and morphological data to infer vowel length, enabling less common word forms to inherit markings from more common ones. A character-level transformer trained on the tool's output matches or exceeds accuracy on a manually annotated benchmark, demonstrating improved performance over rule-based methods. The macronizer also enhances downstream tasks such as verse scansion in prosodic natural language processing.

items.title: Researchers define TextNCA, a hierarchical Neural Cellular Automata model with local attention for language modeling, analyzing its performance on WikiText-103 against Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce TextNCA, a 1D causal windowed-attention implementation of Neural Cellular Automata for language modeling, tested on WikiText-103 with about 30 million parameters. The hierarchical model uses three stages with varying window sizes and shared-weight iterations, but it does not outperform parameter-matched Transformers, serving instead as an analytical tool to understand the impact of local, iterated, and weight-shared computation primitives. The study finds that the model's behavior is largely driven by a staged narrow-to-wide attention schedule, with iteration providing a smaller, bounded benefit optimized at four iterations. Components like the GRU gate and learned per-step embeddings are necessary for this benefit, and training with random iteration counts allows inference-time adjustment at the cost of higher perplexity. The work aims to clarify which aspects of Neural Cellular Automata computations contribute most to language modeling performance.

items.title: Researchers propose SPEE framework for self-improving large language models through progressive experience evolution and policy optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce SPEE (Self-Progressive Experience Evolution), a post-training framework designed to enable large language models (LLMs) to self-improve by transforming transient interaction experiences into persistent capabilities. SPEE combines explicit experience evolution, which extracts and refines knowledge from multiple interaction trajectories, with implicit policy optimization using reinforcement learning to explore new strategies. This approach addresses limitations in existing self-improvement methods that either extract experience without internalizing it or update model parameters without accumulating transferable experience. SPEE maintains a global experience pool that consolidates knowledge from both successful and failed attempts, filters out low-utility experiences, and reduces biases from individual trajectories. Experiments on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that SPEE outperforms existing test-time and training-time self-evolution baselines across three model scales. The researchers have made the source code publicly available for further exploration and validation.

items.title: TRACE-TS introduces attribution-grounded reasoning framework for wearable sensor data, improving human activity understanding with structured evidence and language model-generated reasoning traces [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: TRACE-TS is a new framework designed to enhance human activity recognition from wearable sensor data by generating structured, signal-grounded reasoning traces. It uses attribution from an expert classifier to identify key sensor regions and constructs directed acyclic graph (DAG) reasoning traces with explicit evidence provenance, training a compact language model to generate these traces alongside activity predictions without needing attribution at inference. The framework introduces Semantic Node Match (SNM), a metric that evaluates reasoning fidelity by detecting hallucinated observations and broken evidence chains missed by standard natural language generation metrics. Tested across seven wearable benchmarks, TRACE-TS achieved the highest average accuracy (84.43%) and F1 score (81.24%), outperforming the best large language model-based baseline by 17.96% in F1. The code for TRACE-TS is publicly available.

items.title: Researchers present RMSWeb, a three-part method improving web agent reinforcement learning for Qwen3-VL-Instruct models at 8B and 32B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: RMSWeb addresses challenges in training compact web agents by introducing reflection-conditioned retries to increase data collection efficiency, failure-mode mining to focus offline reinforcement learning on critical states, and Salvage-DS to improve learning signals for rejected action groups. This approach reduces action steps by up to 19.7% on solved tasks and improves performance by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B on benchmarks including WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench. The 8B model achieves the strongest reported results among similarly sized open-weight models on Online-Mind2Web and demonstrates a leading accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, noting differences in external evaluation protocols.

items.title: Researchers present a unified LLMOps architecture integrating real-time data ingestion, continual learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and human feedback to improve large language model deployments in regulated sectors [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a pattern-driven LLMOps architecture that addresses challenges in real-time, regulated deployments of large language models, such as knowledge staleness, catastrophic forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback loops. The architecture combines adaptive ingestion, continual learning, adaptive retrieval policies, and automated feedback-driven convergence into a single operational pipeline. The approach includes four key components: an adaptive ingestion pattern orchestrator evaluated with FreshStreamBench; STAR+FAR continual learning with sparse temporal adapter routing and freshness-aware replay; SAGE, an SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that predicts per-query passage budgets to meet tail-latency targets; and an automated feedback-driven convergence stage with reinforcement learning from human feedback triggers. This design aims to reduce latency, cost, and accuracy trade-offs while supporting auditability and rollback, making it suitable for high-risk sectors like health care and finance.

items.title: Researchers show chain-of-thought monitoring fails against adversaries who rewrite reasoning to hide exploits, dropping detection rates from 95% to under 11% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers demonstrate that chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring, designed to detect reward hacks that appear clean in actions but reveal themselves in reasoning, can be defeated by adversaries who rewrite only the reasoning while keeping commands and outputs unchanged. This approach drastically reduces a monitor's detection rate on targeted subsets, revealing that aggregate accuracy metrics mask near-total failures where CoT monitoring is the sole defense. The attack works across different monitor types and agent models, including live agents, and trace-only defenses recover only part of the evasion since the rewrite remains truthful about actions but falsifies intent. Additional analysis shows that some detection signals are due to detectors rather than genuine monitor understanding, indicating limitations in current CoT monitoring approaches.

items.title: Researchers develop a unified framework for dense language generation algorithms achieving optimal lower-density guarantees with deterministic and randomized methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present a theoretical framework for language generation that ensures generators produce new valid strings from a stream of examples while maintaining validity and novelty. They introduce a simple deterministic algorithm achieving the optimal lower-density guarantee of 1/2 and extend it with randomized algorithms that improve this guarantee to 1-1/e against oblivious adversaries. Their framework also supports multiple orders of output importance simultaneously without loss in performance. The work builds on prior measures of output coverage called lower density, which quantifies the fraction of important outputs generated before appearing in the data. The researchers provide a simpler analysis than previous studies and demonstrate the flexibility of their approach through extensions that accommodate randomization and multiple relevance orders. This contributes to understanding how language generators can reliably and efficiently cover diverse outputs in adversarial settings.

items.title: Researchers develop self-evolving curriculum using Question-begets-Question method to improve reinforcement fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Math-7B on competition math problems, raising pass@1 accuracy from 5.6% to 16.5% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers addressed challenges in teaching a language model competition mathematics by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B, which initially solved only 5.6% of problems. They introduced Question-begets-Question (QbQ), a method that generates diverse problem variants to overcome data scarcity and trained the model using reinforcement learning without relying on ground-truth reasoning traces. Static training with augmented data plateaued at 14.5% accuracy, but a self-evolving curriculum that iteratively retrains on variants of problems the model mostly solves broke this ceiling, reaching 16.5% pass@1 accuracy after 20 rounds with no saturation. The approach counterintuitively showed that training on problems the model can mostly solve leads to improvements and enables the model to tackle harder, unseen problems. This method demonstrates a scalable way to enhance language model performance on complex reasoning tasks despite limited data and absent oracle reasoning traces.

items.title: Study finds no reliable benefit from competitive adversarial self-play in legal reasoning models across multiple tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers tested whether the competitive component of adversarial self-play-where a student model drafts legal arguments and an adversary attacks them, with rewards for surviving attacks-improves legal reasoning. Using a verifiable survival reward system that checks citations, they compared competitive training to non-competitive training across four independent evaluations and a pilot with a stronger adversary, finding no significant advantage for the competitive approach. Early apparent benefits were attributed to small-sample artifacts, and metrics used revealed pitfalls such as collapsing to recall when adversaries ceased citing gold-standard authorities. This negative result aligns with prior findings in coding domains that the value of multi-teacher curricula lies in verifiable environments rather than competition itself.

items.title: Researchers introduce LongCat Sparse Attention, a hardware-algorithm co-designed framework that reduces indexing overhead and memory inefficiency for long-context AI models up to one million tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: LongCat Sparse Attention (LSA) addresses system-level bottlenecks in DeepSeek Sparse Attention by combining streaming-aware indexing, cross-layer indexing, and hierarchical indexing to improve hardware efficiency and reduce computation. The framework achieves performance comparable to full attention across models ranging from 69 billion to 560 billion parameters and supports native training with extremely long context lengths. LSA underpins the development of LongCat-2.0 and is integrated into the open-source LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse model, which includes an updated long-context training corpus to facilitate further research.

items.title: Researchers propose geometry-guided layerwise feed-forward network width allocation in Transformers, improving validation loss over uniform and cosine taper schedules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a method to allocate feed-forward network (FFN) widths in Transformer models based on geometric changes measured during forward passes, rather than using constant widths across layers. They quantify these changes using metrics like correspondence-preserving shift, Gromov-Wasserstein distortion, and persistent homology, and develop an exact fixed-budget optimizer for layerwise width allocation. Testing across seven pretrained language models and training runs with 128M, 256M, and 440M parameters, the geometry-based allocation schedules, especially those using normalized work metrics, consistently reduce mean validation loss compared to uniform width and hand-designed cosine taper schedules. The study finds that raw Euclidean work correlates with residual-norm growth, while Gromov-Wasserstein work aligns better with layer sensitivity, suggesting geometry-informed width allocation can enhance Transformer training efficiency.

items.title: Researchers propose Instruction-Conditioned Exploration with Asymmetric Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation to improve large language model training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Instruction-Conditioned Exploration (ICE), a method that supplements task prompts with distinct instructions during training to increase behavioral diversity in large language models (LLMs). They combine this with an Asymmetric Reinforcement Learning and Self-Distillation (Asymmetric-RL/SD) objective to transfer learned behaviors to the unconditioned test-time policy, enhancing model performance. Applying ICE with the Asymmetric-RL/SD objective to the Qwen3-1.7B model improves pass@1 accuracy on mathematical reasoning tasks by 5.0% at a 4,000-token response length compared to training with DAPO, with gains persisting at an 8,000-token context length. This approach addresses challenges in exploration due to the LLM action-space structure and leverages pre-trained model flexibility to generate diverse training experiences.

items.title: Researchers release OpenDebateEvidence, a 3.5 million-document dataset for argument mining and summarization from American Competitive Debate [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenDebateEvidence is a large-scale dataset compiled from high school and college American Competitive Debate materials, containing over 3.5 million documents with detailed metadata. It aims to support training and evaluation in computational argumentation and is publicly available for research use. The dataset captures complex argumentative structures and has been used to fine-tune state-of-the-art large language models for abstractive summarization, demonstrating its utility across various methods and datasets.

items.title: Research examines large language models' impact on writing and information ecosystems, highlighting AI detector biases and adoption patterns across multiple domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This dissertation explores how large language models (LLMs) are transforming writing and communication by analyzing institutional adoption, usage patterns, and feedback capabilities. It identifies systematic biases introduced by AI detectors that disadvantage writers using non-dominant language varieties, raising equity concerns in AI governance. The study also presents algorithmic methods to measure LLM adoption across various writing domains, including academic peer reviews, scientific publications, and corporate communications. Additionally, it evaluates LLMs' potential to provide manuscript feedback, particularly benefiting early-career and under-resourced researchers who face challenges in accessing timely reviews.

items.title: Researchers introduce Self-Correction Bench to reveal a 64.5% self-correction blind spot in large language models, showing models correct external but not internal errors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed Self-Correction Bench, a framework that distinguishes whether large language models (LLMs) fail to correct errors due to inability or lack of activation. Testing 14 open-source models revealed a 64.5% blind spot where models corrected externally attributed errors but failed on identical internal errors, indicating the capability exists but is not triggered. The study traced this issue to the absence of error-correction sequences in fine-tuning data and showed that fine-tuning with just over 5,000 such sequences reduced the blind spot by 76%. Additionally, appending the word "Wait" to prompts reduced the blind spot by 89.3% without additional training, suggesting multiple mechanisms govern self-correction activation.

items.title: Researchers propose interpretable AI model using weighted structured patterns to detect cognitive distortions in natural language texts, improving F1 scores on two public datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed a new approach for multi-factor classification of natural language texts that uses weighted structured patterns like N-grams and accounts for heterarchical relationships between them. This method aims to automate the detection of specific cognitive distortions relevant to psychological care through an interpretable, robust, and transparent AI model. The proposed recognition and learning algorithms demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods, as tested on two publicly available datasets with optimized hyper-parameters. The team has made the code and models available for community use.

items.title: Researchers introduce LatentMAS, a training-free framework enabling direct latent space collaboration among large language model agents, improving accuracy and efficiency across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed LatentMAS, a framework that allows large language model (LLM) agents to collaborate directly within continuous latent space rather than relying on text-based communication. This approach uses auto-regressive latent thought generation and a shared latent working memory to preserve and transfer internal representations without re-encoding, aiming to enhance expressiveness and reduce complexity compared to traditional text-based multi-agent systems. Empirical evaluations on nine benchmarks covering math, science reasoning, commonsense understanding, and code generation demonstrate that LatentMAS outperforms advanced single agents and text-based multi-agent baselines, achieving up to 14.6% higher accuracy, reducing output token usage by 70.8% to 83.7%, and providing fourfold faster end-to-end inference. The code and data for LatentMAS have been fully open-sourced for further research and development.

items.title: Researchers apply diffusion tensor imaging to visualize information flow in word embeddings across large language model layers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present a novel method using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to analyze and visualize how information flows in natural language expressions within large language models (LLMs). This approach tracks changes in embedding space representations between tokens, offering insights beyond traditional single-word embedding visualizations and improving model interpretability. The method enables comparison of different LLM structures and may help identify under-utilized layers for potential pruning. Their findings suggest that DTI-based visualization provides a deeper understanding of how LLMs represent natural language in context.

items.title: MAPLE introduces metadata-augmented in-context learning to improve differentially private synthetic data generation for domain-specific language models, reducing API costs and improving convergence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: MAPLE addresses the challenge of differentially private fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) when direct model access is unavailable by generating synthetic data grounded in private tabular metadata. This method enhances Private Evolution (PE) by using metadata to better initialize synthetic data distributions, improving alignment with specialized domain data and overcoming convergence and utility issues common in prior approaches. Evaluations on domain-specific text generation tasks demonstrate that MAPLE achieves a superior privacy-utility trade-off, converges faster, and significantly lowers API usage costs compared to baseline PE methods. This approach enables practical, privacy-preserving adaptation of LLMs via API-based frameworks without requiring full model access or extensive compute resources.

items.title: LangFIR identifies sparse language-specific features from monolingual data to improve language steering in multilingual large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: LangFIR is a method that discovers sparse, language-specific features in large language models using only small amounts of monolingual data and random-token sequences, enabling more reliable control of output language. It filters out language-agnostic features to isolate those that are highly selective and causally important for specific languages, improving multilingual generation accuracy across multiple models, datasets, and languages. The approach outperforms previous methods relying on parallel data, suggesting that language identity in multilingual models is localized in sparse feature directions discoverable without expensive multilingual resources.

items.title: Researchers introduce Tensor Mixture (MixT), a Hamiltonian-inspired local-operator ansatz to reduce parameters and computation in large language models like Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Tensor Mixture (MixT), a method inspired by quantum many-body physics that represents dense neural network maps as sums of overlapping local tensor operators, aiming to reduce parameter and computational burdens in large language models. They tested MixT on Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B models, finding a broad regime where accuracy is maintained before a sharp, model-specific boundary where performance changes abruptly. This approach also reduces arithmetic, storage, and memory requirements while revealing structural properties of learned linear maps at billion-parameter scale.

items.title: Researchers study machine unlearning through mode connectivity, revealing connected model basins and nonlinear unlearning progression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers analyze machine unlearning by examining mode connectivity, the phenomenon where independently trained models connect via smooth low-loss paths in parameter space. They introduce mode connectivity in unlearning (MCU) and evaluate it across various settings, finding that many unlearned models reside in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior, while training dynamics can shift solutions into different basins. MCU also shows that models within the same basin can differ significantly on privacy metrics and that unlearning progresses nonlinearly from the original to the unlearned model. The study finds that linear connectivity suggests most approximate unlearning methods differ mechanistically from retraining. Additionally, MCU-based ensembling can enhance generalization and robustness against relearning attacks, and MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty. This work represents the first investigation of machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity, providing new insights into the loss landscape and optimization geometry of unlearning.

items.title: Researchers propose a semantic retrieval framework to measure LLM generation novelty at pretraining scale, revealing longer sequence dependencies and effects of instruction tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a three-stage semantic retrieval framework to efficiently measure generation novelty in large language models (LLMs) against full pretraining corpora, addressing limitations of lexical overlap methods. Applying this to the SmolLM model family, they find that models reference pretraining data over longer sequences than previously known, that task domains influence novelty levels, and that instruction tuning increases novelty beyond style changes. The team released approximately 20 terabytes of corpus chunks and index artifacts to support reproducibility and further research.

items.title: Researchers propose almost orthogonal feature constraints to reduce interference in language model interventions, improving modularity and preserving performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers address the challenge of feature entanglement in language models, which causes interference during localized interventions on linear features representing meaningful concepts. They propose constraining internal features to be almost orthogonal, promoting modular representations that support more isolated causal interventions. The study formalizes the relationship between ideal isolated interventions and actual effects, bounding feature interference propagation through self-coherence measures and introducing orthogonality regularization on the feature dictionary. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach enables more precise interventions on mathematical reasoning concepts without degrading model performance.

items.title: Researchers propose HIVE framework for hierarchical pre-training of vision encoders with large language models, improving vision-language alignment and outperforming self-attention methods on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce HIVE, a novel framework that enhances vision-language alignment by integrating hierarchical cross-attention between vision encoders and large language models (LLMs). This approach enables structured feature fusion across multiple layers, improving gradient flow and representation learning compared to conventional methods that flatten image embeddings. HIVE employs a three-stage training strategy to progressively align the vision encoder with the LLM, ensuring stable optimization and effective multimodal fusion. Empirical evaluations show that HIVE achieves superior performance in image classification and various vision-language tasks, outperforming self-attention-based methods on benchmarks such as MME, GQA, OK-VQA, and ScienceQA, highlighting the benefits of hierarchical feature integration for more efficient and expressive vision-language models.

items.title: Researchers present Key-Value Means, a transformer architecture with expandable block-recurrent compressed memory enabling fixed-size or growing state and efficient long-context performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Key-Value Means (KVM), a novel block-recurrent attention mechanism for transformers that supports either fixed-size or growable memory states, combining benefits of transformers and recurrent neural networks. KVM enables efficient long-context processing with subquadratic prefill time and sublinear state growth while maintaining chunk-wise parallelizable training and prefill without custom kernels. The approach equips transformers with fixed-size KVM attention layers to create strong chunked RNNs with linear time complexity and minimal additional parameters. KVM can be applied at every layer to save memory and offers a continuous range of prefill time complexities between linear and quadratic. The authors have released their code and trained models under the Apache 2.0 license.

items.title: Researchers find length penalties in chain-of-thought reasoning reduce monitorability despite preserving accuracy in Qwen3 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers trained Qwen3 4B and 14B models with penalties on chain-of-thought length to reduce inference costs and overthinking, finding that shorter reasoning chains mention misleading hints less often but still allow those hints to influence answers. They evaluated the models on MMLU Pro R data and four transfer benchmarks, observing that compression reduces reasoning tokens and maintains most multiple-choice accuracy, but lowers faithfulness and hint detection rates significantly at the shortest chain lengths. By comparing compressed chains to length-matched baselines with randomly deleted sentences, they showed that compression removes more evidence than shorter traces alone would predict, identifying a trade-off frontier between reasoning cost reduction and monitorability.

items.title: Researchers propose OTAP, a structure-aware optimal transport metric for evaluating agent trajectories in planning and execution tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce OTAP (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), a new metric that evaluates large language model agent trajectories by measuring distance between execution graphs and valid solution graphs using an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport approach. OTAP is designed to be invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings and robust to missing or hallucinated steps, addressing limitations of existing metrics that rely on binary success flags or exact matching. On benchmarks and controlled tests, OTAP effectively distinguishes valid from invalid trajectories, especially in open-ended domains without formal verifiers, where traditional surface metrics perform less reliably.

items.title: Researchers formulate cognitive experiment design as a Bayesian Experimental Design problem, introducing an amortized framework to efficiently infer cognition parameters across varying environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This paper presents a method to optimize cognitive experiments for inferring latent cognitive mechanisms by treating the experimental environment as a design variable within a Bayesian Experimental Design framework. The authors develop an amortized approach that approximates exact Monte Carlo benchmarks with reduced computational cost, demonstrating its effectiveness on the Mouselab-MDP process-tracing paradigm. Their findings reveal that no single experimental environment is optimal for all inference objectives, highlighting trade-offs among information gain, posterior recoverability, and efficiency. This work provides a principled approach to selecting informative environments for Bayesian cognition parameter inference.

items.title: Researchers propose SCMA, a structure-conditioned and metal-aware Flow Matching method to reduce metal artifacts in CT scans, improving artifact suppression and anatomical preservation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Metallic objects in X-ray CT scans cause artifacts that hinder clinical diagnosis and analysis. Existing metal artifact reduction methods have limitations such as residual artifacts, poor generalization, or anatomical inconsistencies. The proposed SCMA framework integrates sample-specific structural conditions and metal-aware spatial weighting into Flow Matching, combined with projection-consistency correction, to better suppress metal artifacts while preserving anatomical structures. SCMA uses a linear-interpolation-corrected image as a structural guide and incorporates time-varying spatial weights based on metal masks to focus on severely degraded regions. Experiments on simulated and real CT data show that SCMA outperforms representative metal artifact reduction methods by reducing artifacts and hallucination-like structures inconsistent with measured projections.

items.title: Study finds perceived national origin of large language models does not affect their persuasive power in US debates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A preregistered randomized experiment with 403 US adults found that labeling a chatbot as American or Chinese did not influence attitude changes or argumentative behavior during political and non-political debates. Participants interacted with the same GPT-4o model instructed to argue against their initial positions, and substantial attitude shifts occurred regardless of the chatbot's presented nationality. The only notable effect was lower pre-conversation human-like trust in the chatbot labeled as Chinese, while trust in its functionality remained unchanged. Political topics slowed agreement with the AI's stance, and collective narcissism reduced attitude change overall, suggesting that origin labeling alone may not effectively guard against foreign influence through conversational AI.

items.title: Researchers propose Entropy-Scaled Trust Region to improve asynchronous reinforcement learning stability and speed in large language model training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers address instability in asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model post-training caused by stale, off-policy data leading to policy collapse. They identify that importance ratio scales vary with token entropy, causing noise amplification at low entropy and exploratory deviations at high entropy, which existing magnitude-only corrections mishandle. To solve this, they introduce the Entropy-Scaled Trust Region (ESTR) method that scales off-policy deviations by local entropy without extra forward passes or version detection. ESTR outperforms existing asynchronous methods on long-horizon agentic tasks and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, matching synchronous GRPO performance while achieving a 2.6× speedup.

items.title: RubricReviewer introduces a rubric-driven framework combining training-free and trained models to improve AI-assisted peer review comprehensiveness and robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: RubricReviewer addresses limitations in existing large language model (LLM) peer reviewers by explicitly generating paper-adaptive rubrics as an intermediate step, separating rubric derivation from judgment. It combines a training-free agent that gathers external evidence with a human-aligned trained model that consumes this evidence, enhancing review comprehensiveness and discriminative power. Experiments on real-world submissions demonstrate that RubricReviewer produces more comprehensive and discriminative reviews than prior systems and shows strong robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks. Ablation studies confirm the importance of each component in the framework.

items.title: AgentMemBench benchmarks five long-term memory strategies for conversational AI, finding external key-value stores outperform others on recall and faithfulness across multiple datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AgentMemBench introduces a unified benchmark to evaluate five long-term memory management strategies for conversational AI agents, including in-context windowing, external key-value stores, graph-based episodic memory, compression-based summarisation, and web-augmented memory. The benchmark assesses these methods on three public datasets covering multi-session dialogue, task-oriented document grounding, and persona-grounded chat, using metrics such as Recall@k, MRR, and faithfulness scores over 491 annotated question turns. Results show that external key-value stores dominate in recall and faithfulness, especially for long-range recall where other methods perform poorly. Compression-based summarisation ranks second in retrieval quality, while web-augmented memory matches in-corpus recall but lacks provenance. The superior recall of external key-value stores comes with a higher memory footprint, highlighting an accuracy-efficiency trade-off. The study also evaluates two existing memory systems and releases all code and data for reproducibility.

items.title: Researchers present DLLM-TTS, a block discrete diffusion language model for efficient text-to-speech synthesis with parallel token prediction and competitive performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce DLLM-TTS, a text-to-speech framework that uses conditional block discrete diffusion over neural audio codec tokens to balance speed and linguistic accuracy. The model processes sequences in blocks with masked diffusion, enabling parallel token prediction during inference and achieving a real-time factor of 0.15. A 0.6 billion-parameter DLLM-TTS model trained on 20,000 hours of data demonstrates competitive results on the Seed-TTS-eval benchmark, suggesting that block discrete diffusion language models can provide practical, data-efficient speech synthesis with parallel generation capabilities.

items.title: Researchers propose Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law to predict vision-language model performance from textual capabilities across 7 LLM families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce the Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law, a framework that predicts vision-language model (VLM) accuracy based on textual capability scores derived from large language models (LLMs). They trained over 150 VLMs using 34 LLMs from 7 model families and evaluated performance on more than 200 textual and 50 multimodal benchmarks, demonstrating accurate extrapolation and generalization across model families. The study reveals that base LLMs outperform instruction-tuned models as VLM backbones due to better data absorption and scaling efficiency, and identifies certain textual benchmarks that negatively correlate with multimodal performance, indicating potential benchmark-gaming. This framework aims to make backbone selection for VLMs a principled, quantitative process rather than relying on costly empirical testing. Code and data are publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce activation-steering workflow for role-conditioned language model agents in social simulations, improving role-profile alignment on OLMo-3-7B-Instruct [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present an activation-steering screening workflow to condition language model agents on specific roles before deploying them in social simulations. The method involves defining role profiles, extracting role-specific directions, adjusting steering coefficients, and evaluating alignment, applied to a 275-role inventory using OLMo-3-7B-Instruct and GPT-4.1-mini for role references and judgments. Role-specific steering improved alignment scores significantly compared to prior persona-vector controls while maintaining lexical diversity. The study found that while most roles benefited from increased steering, some declined, highlighting the need for role-specific coefficient tuning rather than uniform settings. The researchers have made their code and evaluation materials publicly available.

items.title: Exploring More to Solve More: Boosting Diversity in Text Diffusion Models via Entropy-Based Guidance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although diffusion models have revolutionized continuous domains like image synthesis through high quality generations and controllable guidance mechanisms, bringing this controllability to the discrete, sequential nature of text remains an open challenge. Meanwhile, current sampling strategies and guidance methods adjust token likelihoods without capturing the broader semantic landscape, leading to a suboptimal balance between fidelity and diversity. In this work, we introduce a novel training-free Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy (SAKE) guidance method. Our method computes the order-2 R\'enyi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix that captures both cross-token semantic interactions and relative token positions. By linearizing this objective in the embedding space, we derive a tractable guidance signal that dynamically adjusts the sampling distribution, flattening it to encourage exploration during redundancy and sharpening it for fidelity when diverse. Empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior Pareto frontier between fidelity and diversity, and improves multi-sample performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, such as code and mathematics generation, compared to temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines.

items.title: SLMs as Multi-Agent Routers: A Progressive SFT and Reinforcement Learning Approach [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Specialised retrieval agents typically surface higher quality results than general-purpose search, but selecting the optimal agent for a given query remains an open problem. Current approaches route queries based on inferred topic or intent, however intent-based selection is fundamentally limited: it does not incorporate signal from retrieved content, and cannot detect when a topically aligned agent produces low-relevance results. We address this by training a small language model via supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning to jointly perform agent selection and structured parameter generation for downstream tool calls, using a hierarchical reward function grounded in retrieval relevance along with query-agent topic alignment. This enables the model to learn task-dependent agent suitability from retrieval performance: which agents reliably yield high-relevance results for which query distributions, and when to redirect queries away from specialised agents despite surface-level topical overlap. On a targeted subset of such agent-query mismatches, the trained model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.918 compared to 0.539 and 0.490 for two LLM baselines (Amazon Nova Lite and Claude Haiku 4.5) that route on intent alone. Overall, it achieves a mean NDCG@10 of 0.771 (+0.177 over Nova Lite, +0.219 over Haiku) with a mean selection latency of 120.1ms, an 82.4% reduction over Nova Lite.

items.title: XL-DocBench: Benchmarking Evidence-Grounded Extra-Long Document Understanding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world document tasks often ask professionals to answer questions from annual reports, regulations, clinical guidelines, and technical manuals that span hundreds or thousands of pages. Some questions also require comparing related reports. Reliable long-document understanding is therefore a prerequisite for using LLMs in compliance, clinical, financial, and engineering workflows, where decisions must be traceable to specific evidence pages and the cost of an unsupported answer is high -- yet most existing benchmarks still measure short-context or single-page QA. We introduce XL-DocBench, a fully human-verified benchmark for extra-long document understanding, with 1,519 retained questions from six professional domains and contexts up to 2,303 pages. XL-DocBench goes beyond page-level lookup. 1,103 examples (72.6\%) use multiple evidence pages. The final set also includes 556 questions (36.6\%) that use tables, charts, or figures, and 165 questions (10.9\%) that require evidence from multiple documents. Each question has one of twelve reasoning labels, expert-annotated evidence pages, a typed verification rule, and an answer format, including 218 None-answer cases. We build the benchmark with a tree-guided synthesis pipeline followed by artifact filters and full verification by 194 human experts. By coupling extra-long professional contexts with page-level evidence and typed rules, XL-DocBench fills a gap left by prior single-page, short multi-page, or text-only long-context benchmarks, and lets future work attribute system failures to retrieval, evidence use, or rule following rather than to a single leaderboard score. The results show that current systems still struggle with long contexts, multi-page evidence, and structured reasoning over professional documents.

items.title: Trustworthiness Costs of Domain Adaptation in Small Language Models:A Cross-Architecture Empirical Study [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Domain adaptation of small language models (SLMs) has emerged as a practical strategy for deploying capable NLP systems in resource-constrained, high-stakes environments including healthcare, legal services, and financial analysis. While performance gains from parameter-efficient fine-tuning are well characterised, the corresponding impact on trustworthiness (factual calibration and adversarial robustness) remains poorly understood. This paper presents the first systematic cross-domain, cross-architecture empirical study quantifying the trustworthiness cost of domain adaptation across three SLM architectures (TinyLlama 1B, Gemma-2 2B, Llama 3.2 1B), three domains (healthcare, legal, finance), two training-data conditions (benign and adversarially perturbed), and four fine-tuning strategies (baseline LoRA, Safety-DPO, Dark Experience Replay, and Task Arithmetic LoRA, TA-LoRA). Trustworthiness is evaluated through TruthfulQA MC2 (factual calibration) and HarmBench ASR (adversarial robustness) across all 216 experimental configurations with three random seeds. Three principal findings emerge. First, baseline QLoRA domain adaptation produces minimal TruthfulQA MC2 change across all model-domain combinations (mean |Delta TQA| < 0.02). Second, adversarially perturbed training data consistently improves domain adaptation quality (Delta loss approximately -0.040) without worsening trustworthiness benchmarks. Third, none of the three safety-preserving strategies reduced adversarial harm susceptibility: Safety-DPO was effectively neutral (mean Delta ASR < 0.001), while Dark ER and TA-LoRA increased mean HarmBench ASR by +0.171 and +0.155 respectively in safety-aligned models (Gemma-2 2B, Llama 3.2 1B), with individual configurations exceeding +0.45. These results challenge the assumption that replay-based and arithmetic-merge strategies transfer alignment to domain-adapted SLMs.

items.title: Neural Circuit Function Inference with LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The success of connectome mapping now shifts the challenge of understanding the nervous system to the interpretation of neural circuits. Here, we devise a new automated method, LLantia (LLM automated neural circuit inference and analysis), to systematically infer neural circuit function and the role of its component neural cell types. Our approach distills descriptions of cell type function from the literature and, in combination with the connectome, then infers the function for all other cell types, which serves as a basis for subsequent neural circuit function inference. Results are structured hierarchically, with different possible circuit functions organised under multiple possible behavioural and physiological contexts, and each circuit function composed of subcircuit descriptions alongside relevant cell types to facilitate both backtracking to known, published information and support further experimental research. We illustrate our method by inferring cell type function for all cell types of the adult fruit fly brain and for select broader circuits within, and validate our findings, including by cross-checking with literature published after the release date of our analysis.

items.title: DiffusionGemma Technical Report [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce DiffusionGemma, an experimental open-weight language model that uses discrete diffusion to generate text at exceptionally high speed. Rather than decoding one token at a time, DiffusionGemma iteratively refines blocks of 256 tokens in parallel, avoiding the sequential decoding bottleneck of conventional autoregressive (AR) large language models. Instead of training from scratch, we obtain DiffusionGemma by fine-tuning the mixture-of-experts Gemma 4 model with 3.8B activated and 25.2B total parameters. Our compute-efficient two-stage training pipeline uses fewer than 10% of the starting AR model's total training token budget. The first stage uses supervised fine-tuning to teach bidirectional denoising, while the second stage combines reinforcement learning with sampler distillation to jointly improve generation quality and inference efficiency. DiffusionGemma establishes a new Pareto frontier for the trade-off between generation speed and model capability. Averaged across our full evaluation suite, it generates around 20 tokens per forward pass and achieves roughly 1,500 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, which is substantially faster than AR models even with state-of-the-art speculative decoding. DiffusionGemma also retains the starting model's support for thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long contexts. Despite diffusion fine-tuning, it remains capable of AR generation with only minor performance degradation, suggesting a path toward hybrid diffusion-AR decoding.

items.title: A Constitution-Grid Instrument for Data-Efficient RL Alignment (C-Guard) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conflicting objectives are general in RL alignment, and training on them data-efficiently is hard. Training a safety guard with RL means optimizing two objectives that conflict: catch real harm, and do not refuse benign prompts. Our finding is that over-refusal improves 22.4% to 12.8%, while under-refusal on adversarial attacks silently worsens 0.27 to 0.33. We present C-Guard, a constitution-grid instrument that generates the RL training data, and C-LIM, a per-cell learnability score that decides each cell's move: prune, densify, amend, expand. C-LIM flags the dead-weight data region before any training budget is spent: 187 untargeted rows had bought zero gain, and our method lifts the same region's learning impact 0.733 to 0.80. Code and the constitution are open-sourced.

items.title: Cross-Task Dissociation in Frontier Vision-Language Model Theory of Mind [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do frontier vision-language models present a coherent Theory-of-Mind (ToM) profile across tasks, matching the same human reference group, or does that profile fragment from one paradigm to the next? We evaluate a shared panel of nine frontier VLMs on two psychology-derived benchmarks: the Keysar Director Task (visual perspective-taking under egocentric interference) and the Frith-Happ\'e animated triangles scored with the Castelli rubric (intention attribution from pure motion). On the Director Task, without chain-of-thought, the panel makes the egocentric error on 78\% of trials like children rather than adults; variation is substantial across models, and reasoning rescues several models. On the triangles, the panel under-attributes intention: its ToM profile sits more than three times closer to the high-functioning-autistic-adult (HF-ASD) mean than to the typical-development-adult (TD) mean, while Goal-Directed and Random stay near TD. No model is nearest TD on both tasks; the model that looks adult-like on the Director Task falls on the HF-ASD side on the triangles, and the most TD-like model on the triangles is child-like on the Director Task. We report group-level descriptions, not diagnostic labels for any model.

items.title: Sixteen models, fewer than two voices: measuring ensemble dispersion where no answer is uniquely correct [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sixteen language models drawn from ten families produced, on average, the semantic diversity of 1.69 distinct formulations of a psychotherapeutic case, against a single-model baseline of 1.43 from one model's own runs. Ensembles place more than one reading before a decision-maker on the premise that several models supply several perspectives. Dispersion over their outputs is measured both as diversity and as uncertainty, and both traditions validate it against a correctness criterion that this task does not admit. Measuring diversity is a solved problem: the Vendi Score, the exponential of the von Neumann entropy of a similarity matrix, is an effective number of distinct elements. What a single aggregate does not say is where the diversity comes from. We define a per-model dissent contribution, the complement of a model's mean similarity to the other members of its ensemble: a magnitude from the same matrix, not a decomposition of the spectral index, whose maximum identifies the most divergent voice. Crossing model and case, we test as a preregistered hypothesis whether model identity accounts for a non-zero share of the variance in dissent, and characterise the structure that test detects. The panel formulated fifteen stratified vignettes, yielding 7,082 formulations for analysis. Model identity was a detectable structuring factor of the dissent that remained, but the usual categories recovered it only partly: scale differences pointed in opposite directions across pairs, family grouped models on only five two-member lines, and the most divergent voice changed with panel composition, so that the surfaced outlier describes the ensemble rather than the model. Dissent did not track the interpretive openness for which the case bank was stratified; it was organised by clinical content instead, leaving the dispersion an ensemble produces a property to measure rather than assume.

items.title: CurveShift: Is Agent Progress Scalar? Separating Level from Shape [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Progress in large language models is often summarized using a single scalar measure, such as a time horizon, a latent ability estimate, or an aggregate benchmark score. These summaries capture the overall performance, but they do not test whether progress is distributed differently across task difficulty. We find that most of the apparent shift in gains toward harder tasks does not reflect a change in the shape of the difficulty-response curve. On METR time-horizon data, a single Rasch model with rising ability reproduces this pattern, so it is largely explained by ceiling effects rather than a qualitative change in capability. This echoes how the choice of metric can make claimed emergent abilities look like a property of the models themselves. We then identify a smaller hard-task effect that survives this control. Isolating it is difficult on agentic benchmarks, because newer models are usually run with newer agentic harnesses, so a gain on hard tasks cannot be assigned to the model or its scaffold. We break the confound with LiveCodeBench, a public competitive programming benchmark that runs no agentic scaffold while pairing dated models with an exogenous difficulty ordering. After accounting for the rise in overall ability, models released after September 2024 still gain on the hardest problems beyond what their easy and medium performance predicts, by about +0.40 logits under our most conservative assumption, raising the hard-problem solve rate from roughly 18% to 25%. The effect is led by the strongest reasoning models and holds for hard tasks that need only short reasoning, not autonomy over long horizons. We present this as a result specific to competitive programming, since our clean identification rests on a single coding benchmark. We release the LiveCodeBench Difficulty Panel (66 dated models x 1,055 problems) and our analysis code.

items.title: AdaMTP: An Adaptive Training Paradigm for Multi-Token Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) has emerged as an effective paradigm that augments a shared Large Language Model backbone with auxiliary heads, training the model to predict several future tokens in parallel to enrich its supervision signal and accelerate inference. However, existing training frameworks adopt a rigid, fixed-length prediction horizon, disregarding the highly non-uniform information density of natural language and code. Forcing the auxiliary heads to predict across high-entropy semantic boundaries injects noisy, conflicting training signals; because these heads share the backbone's latent representations, the resulting gradients backpropagate and interfere with the model's core capabilities. We propose AdaMTP, an adaptive training paradigm that dynamically aligns the prediction horizon with the intrinsic predictability of the sequence. At its core, an entropy-based segmentation algorithm leverages the base model to detect sudden surges in uncertainty as semantic boundaries, partitioning sequences into variable-length groups. Each token is assigned an adaptive prediction depth, and a dynamically masked MTP objective suppresses the loss for predictions that cross these boundaries, attenuating the noisy gradients that degrade the backbone. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general benchmarks on three backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-12B), AdaMTP consistently outperforms standard MTP in both task performance and inference speedup.

items.title: Rethinking and formalising the state across languages: a unified computational learning theory account [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The linguistic notion of state has traditionally been restricted to the construct (annexation) state of Afroasiatic languages and treated as a language-specific morphosyntactic phenomenon. This article argues instead that the state is a systemic, context-dependent morphosyntactic mechanism that selects grammatical templates across synthetic languages. Within the Template-Based Modular Cognitive framework, taking Riffian as its primary empirical basis, the proposed theory provides a unified explanation for diverse nominal marking patterns traditionally analysed independently and is formalised as a symbolic computational model in which the state is represented by a set-valued function over grammatical templates. A learning algorithm based on finite-set operations acquires and predicts state-dependent grammatical configurations. Beyond nominal morphology, the framework has broader implications for theories of nominal structure and lexical cognition, in particular offering a unified analysis of determiner-noun structure. These results suggest that the state constitutes one instance of a broader class of syntactically conditioned dependencies that also includes agreement and grammatical case.

items.title: Loanword or Switch? The Annotation Boundary, Not the Model, Drives Kazakh-Russian Code-Switching Identification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Off-the-shelf LID and letter heuristics over-label Kazakh-Russian social text as mixed: Russian loanwords inside Kazakh look like code-switching under a shared Cyrillic script. We release a document-level gold LID set whose guideline keeps integrated borrowings as Kazakh and reserves mixed for clause-level switches, plus a mixed-only sentiment pool used after LID in a filter-first cascade. On a shared LID test, FastText, Lingua, raw and windowed HeLI, character-trigram NB, and XLM-R range from weak to strong performance. The gap shows the bottleneck is the loanword-vs-switch annotation boundary, not model class alone.

items.title: Verification Without Sufficiency: Per-Chunk Filtering Fails on Multi-Hop RAG, and Decomposition Repairs It [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verification for retrieval-augmented generation usually scores each retrieved chunk and drops the ones that fail. We show this cannot work for multi-hop questions, and show what does. Per-chunk scoring assumes one chunk is a sufficient premise for the answer. Multi-hop questions are built so that none is, and the paragraph carrying the answer is the one the question does not name. Entailment scoring reaches 0.643, 0.523 and 0.560 AUC on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue, against 0.951 on single-hop SQuAD. Seven controls rule out model capacity, premise length, hypothesis template, decision threshold, retriever, answer-matching criterion and prompt. End to end across three datasets, three generator sizes and two prompts, per-chunk gating is significantly worse than not filtering at all in every cell, and its penalty grows with generator capability. The repair is to condition verification on the decomposed sub-question rather than the original query. Using MuSiQue's gold decomposition, entailment on a later hop rises from 0.546, which is chance, to 0.840, a paired lift of +0.355 with a bootstrap interval of [0.331, 0.382]. An off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-7B decomposer, given the question and the top retrieved paragraph, reaches 0.637 and captures 31% of that ceiling; decomposing without retrieval reaches 0.533, below the original question. Iterative retrieval systems already produce such decompositions and discard them before verifying.

items.title: Pruned BPE: Post-training Visibility Pruning and Token Reallocation for Byte Pair Encoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.00837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is widely used for subword tokenization, but standard BPE exposes every learned merge token to the downstream model, including tokens that mainly serve as intermediate construction units and rarely appear in the final encoded corpus. This paper proposes Pruned BPE, a post-training visibility-pruning and token-reallocation method that separates merge construction from model-visible vocabulary selection. After standard BPE training, tokens are evaluated by final exposure. Low-exposure tokens are retained as internal-only merge nodes, while their visible vocabulary slots are reassigned to better-exposed candidates learned through resumed training. During encoding, internal-only tokens are recursively expanded into visible descendants while the original BPE merge order is preserved. Experiments on two non-overlapping English- and Chinese-dominated corpora and their combination show that Pruned BPE consistently reduces encoded length relative to Standard BPE at the same training corpus, evaluation corpus, and model-visible vocabulary size. At a 40\% exposure threshold, the reduction is approximately 0.27\%--0.36\% on same-corpus evaluations. In a vocabulary-only evaluation using a shared exact minimum-token dynamic-programming encoder, Pruned BPE retains an advantage of approximately 0.23\%--0.31\%, indicating that the improvement arises from a more efficient visible vocabulary. These gains represent a meaningful fraction of the approximately 1.5\%--3.8\% marginal reduction that would otherwise require adding another 2K Standard BPE tokens. Qualitative analysis shows that internal-only tokens include reusable English fragments, Chinese components, partial UTF-8 byte sequences, and structured-text fragments. The results indicate that post-training visibility pruning can improve BPE vocabulary efficiency without increasing the vocabulary exposed to the language model.

items.title: MedUPS: Towards Diagnostic Assistance in Uncommon Medical Cases with Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.01012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncommon and off-guideline cases are difficult for clinical decision support, because physicians must make a series of management decisions under diagnostic uncertainty and rarely see the full case at once. Most large language model (LLM) benchmarks for medicine score only the final diagnosis, yet much of clinical care turns on the next appropriate action: the next test to order, the imaging study to obtain, the specialist to involve, or the differential to pursue. We introduce MedUPSQA, a dataset of 21,874 mid-stream clinical decision points built from 5,535 real case reports, and MedUPS, an alignment framework that supervises models on these intermediate decisions as they unfold along a patient's trajectory. We segment free-text case presentations into chronologically ordered, accumulating clinical chunks and align models to predict the next step with reinforcement learning (GRPO), using an external LLM-as-a-Judge reward. This objective mirrors how clinicians actually meet patients, reasoning forward from accumulating evidence toward the next decision, rather than committing to a final label. Across three backbones, mid-stream alignment raises next-step accuracy from 55.2 to 66.7 for Qwen3.6-27B, from 47.2 to 57.8 for Qwen3.5-9B, and from 37.8 to 44.4 for HuatuoGPT-3-8B, with 95% CI. In several model scales we test the objective improves accuracy more than scale, with smaller models surpassing larger, frontier models we evaluate. We further train supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on the mid-stream task, SFT improves all backbones above base, indicating the target framwork carries signal independently of the optimizer. We release the dataset, code, and aligned checkpoints.

items.title: Cloud-ScPO: Hidden-State Geometry for Semi-Supervised Preference Optimization in LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.01014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preference optimization improves mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs), but reliable chosen-rejected pairs usually require verified answers, human annotations, or external reward models. We investigate whether preference supervision can instead be derived from the model's internal representation geometry in a semi-supervised setting. Our analysis shows that reasoning trajectories generated across different mathematical problems form structured global point clouds in which correct and incorrect trajectories exhibit different geometric organization. Based on this observation, we propose Cloud--ScPO, a topology-guided preference-mining framework that uses a small labeled set to construct multiple correct and incorrect reference Clouds. Each trajectory is represented by a mean-pooled hidden state and scored against connectivity-induced components using a component-level soft $k$-nearest-neighbor measure averaged across reference banks. We combine this cross-problem Cloud signal with prompt-level self-consistency: self-consistency determines the answer-level preference direction, while Cloud scoring selects concrete trajectories and filters pairs by their score margin. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH-Numeric across four model settings show that Cloud--ScPO consistently improves over ScPO, with gains of up to 4.49\% on GSM8K and 4.19\% on MATH-Numeric. Pair-level analyses further show that Cloud--ScPO maintains comparable correctness reliability while more effectively separating informative chosen trajectories from incomplete, repetitive, or otherwise low-quality rejected responses.

items.title: Why LLMs Give In: Conversational Factors and Reasoning Behind Medical Sycophancy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.01017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model that abandons a correct medical answer under user pushback is more dangerous than one that was simply wrong, because it lends the credibility of a correct answer to the user's misinformation. Such model behavior, described as medical sycophancy, is usually reported as a single rate per model, but we find it is a property of the conversation, not the model.
